text: Imagine two students preparing for an exam with last year's paper. One memorises every answer word for word; the other works out why each answer is right. On last year's paper they score the same, but on a fresh paper only the second one does well. Models face exactly this choice, and a model that scores perfectly on the data it has seen can still fail badly on the data it has not.

Here is a small experiment. We take a smooth curve, sample a dozen points from it, and add a little noise, the way real measurements always carry some error. Now we fit polynomials of increasing degree. A straight line is too stiff to follow the bend, so it misses the shape entirely; we call that underfitting. A cubic follows the curve nicely. A polynomial of very high degree threads through every single point, but between the points it swings wildly, because it has spent its flexibility on fitting the noise.

Now measure the error two ways: on the training points the model was fitted to, and on fresh test points drawn from the same curve. As the degree grows, the training error only ever falls, because a more flexible model can always fit the same points at least as well. The test error falls at first, then turns and climbs. That rising branch is overfitting, and the bottom of the valley is the model we actually want.

Two quantities explain the shape of that valley. Bias is the error that comes from the model being too simple to represent the truth, like a bathroom scale that always reads two kilos heavy; averaging many readings will never fix it. Variance is how much the fitted curve changes when you collect a fresh sample of data. Redraw the noisy points, refit, and the straight line barely moves, while the wiggly high-degree curve jumps somewhere completely different each time.

For squared error these pieces add up exactly. The expected test error equals the bias squared, plus the variance, plus the noise in the data itself. The noise is a floor that no model can get under, because it is randomness in the measurements, not a pattern. Making a model more flexible lowers its bias but raises its variance, and the best model balances the two at the bottom of the valley.

So what can we do about high variance? The most reliable cure is more data, because many points pin the curve down and leave the wiggles nowhere to hide. Short of that, we can choose a simpler model, or keep the flexible model but penalise it for being wild, an idea called regularisation. Whatever we do, the judge must always be data the model has never seen.

Large language models have billions of parameters, far more than this textbook picture would seem to allow, and very large networks can behave in ways the simple valley does not predict, a pattern researchers call double descent. Yet the practical habit is the same: during training, engineers watch the loss on held-out text, because a widening gap between training and held-out loss is the classic sign of memorising. Next, we look at regularisation in detail.
